problems.signature: class EventEmitter { on, off, once, emit, removeAllListeners }

what: An event emitter lets parts of a program talk without knowing each other. One side says "tell me when login happens" (on); another side says "login happened, here is the user" (emit).
You can remove a listener (off), listen only once (once), or clear everything (removeAllListeners). emit returns whether anyone was listening.
It is the observer pattern; Node's EventEmitter, the DOM's addEventListener and most pub/sub libraries are this idea.

steps: Keep a Map from event name to an array of listeners.
on(name, fn): push fn; return this so calls can be chained.
emit(name, ...args): copy the list first, then call each listener with the args; return true if there was at least one.
off(name, fn): remove one occurrence of that exact function.
once(name, fn): register a wrapper that calls off on itself, then calls fn. Keep a link to fn so off(name, fn) still finds the wrapper.

  sendWelcome removes itself

where: Streams, servers and sockets all emit events.
A small store that tells components when data changes.
An analytics module listens to app events without the app importing it.
When you need a reply (a value back), call a function or use a promise instead of an event.

why: Removing an item from the array you are iterating moves the next item into the current slot, so the loop steps over it.
Iterate over a copy: [...list].

problems.pseudo:
class EventEmitter:
  events = new Map()            // name -> [listeners]

  on(name, fn):    list(name).push(fn); return this
  off(name, fn):
    list = events.get(name) or stop
    i = index of an entry e where e === fn or e.original === fn
    remove it; return this
  once(name, fn):
    wrapper(...args) = { off(name, wrapper); fn(...args) }
    wrapper.original = fn
    on(name, wrapper)
  emit(name, ...args):
    list = events.get(name); if empty -> return false
    for fn of a COPY of list: fn.apply(this, args)
    return true
  removeAllListeners(name?): delete one name, or clear all

what: An LRU cache (Least Recently Used) holds at most capacity items. When it is full and a new key arrives, it throws out the item that was used longest ago.
"Used" means read with get or written with put. Both must be O(1): no searching through a list.
In JavaScript, a Map remembers insertion order. Deleting a key and setting it again moves it to the end (newest), and map.keys().next().value is the oldest. That gives O(1) for everything.

steps: Keep a Map. Its order is the usage order: first = least recently used, last = most recently used.
get(key): if missing, return -1. Otherwise read the value, delete the key and set it again (moves it to the end), return the value.
put(key, value): if the key exists, delete it first. Then set it (it is now newest).
If size > capacity, delete the first key: map.keys().next().value.

problems.pseudo:
class LRUCache(capacity):
  map = new Map()                 // order = usage order (oldest first)

  get(key):
    if key not in map -> return -1
    value = map.get(key)
    map.delete(key); map.set(key, value)   // move to newest
    return value

  put(key, value):
    if key in map -> map.delete(key)
    map.set(key, value)
    if map.size > capacity:
      oldest = map.keys().next().value
      map.delete(oldest)

what: A promise is a box for a value that arrives later. It starts pending and settles once: fulfilled with a value or rejected with a reason. After that it never changes.
then(onFulfilled, onRejected) registers handlers and returns a new promise, settled with whatever the handler returns (or throws). That is what makes chaining work.
Two rules make it feel "right": handlers always run asynchronously (in a microtask), and if a handler returns another promise or thenable, the new promise waits for it.

steps: Store state, value and a list of waiting callbacks. Call the executor with resolve/reject; if the executor throws, reject.
reject(r) and the final step of resolve set the state once (ignore later calls), then run the waiting callbacks.
resolve(x): if x is a thenable, call x.then(resolve, reject) to adopt it; otherwise fulfil with x.

then: return a new MyPromise. Its job: when this one settles, in a queueMicrotask, call the right handler and resolve the new promise with the result (or reject if it throws). A missing handler passes the value/reason through.
catch(f) = then(undefined, f). finally(f) runs f and passes the original value or reason on.

  .catch(e => 'fixed ' + e)    // p4 resolves with 'fixed bad'
  .finally(() => log('done'))  // p5 still resolves with 'fixed bad'

problems.pseudo:
class MyPromise(executor):
  state = 'pending'; value; callbacks = []
  settle(st, v): if state != pending -> return; state = st; value = v; run all callbacks
  resolve(x):
    if x is a thenable -> try x.then(resolve, reject) once; return
    settle('fulfilled', x)
  reject(r): settle('rejected', r)
  try executor(resolve, reject) catch e -> reject(e)

  then(onF, onR):
    return new MyPromise((res, rej) =>
      task = () => queueMicrotask(() =>
        handler = state == fulfilled ? onF : onR
        if handler is not a function -> pass value (res) or reason (rej) through
        else try res(handler(value)) catch e -> rej(e))
      if pending -> callbacks.push(task) else task())
  catch(f)   = then(undefined, f)
  finally(f) = then(v => MyPromise.resolve(f()).then(() => v),
                    e => MyPromise.resolve(f()).then(() => { throw e }))

what: Four ways to wait for many promises: all (every one must succeed), race (the first to settle wins, success or failure), allSettled (wait for all, never fails), and any (the first success wins).
Results keep the input order, not the order in which promises finished. Plain values in the list are treated like already-resolved promises.
Empty input: all and allSettled resolve with [], any rejects with an AggregateError, and race stays pending forever.

steps: Each function returns new Promise(...) and turns the iterable into an array.
Wrap every item with Promise.resolve(item) so plain values work.
all: store each value at its index and count; when the count reaches the length, resolve. Reject on the first rejection.
allSettled: store { status, value | reason } at each index; resolve when all are in. race: resolve/reject with whatever settles first.
any: resolve on the first success; store reasons at their index and, when all have failed, reject with new AggregateError(reasons).

race        -> 2 at 100ms (B settles first)
allSettled  -> [{ok 1}, {ok 2}, {rejected x}] at 300ms
any         -> 2 at 100ms

problems.pseudo:
promiseAll(iterable):
  items = [...iterable]
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    if items empty -> resolve([])
    results = []; done = 0
    items.forEach((item, i) =>
      Promise.resolve(item).then(v =>
        results[i] = v; done++
        if done == items.length -> resolve(results)
      , reject)))

promiseAllSettled: same, but store {status:'fulfilled', value} / {status:'rejected', reason}, never reject
promiseRace:  each item: Promise.resolve(item).then(resolve, reject)
promiseAny:   first success -> resolve; reasons[i] on failure;
              when all failed (or empty) -> reject(new AggregateError(reasons, 'All promises were rejected'))

what: You have 100 uploads (or API calls) to do. Doing them one by one is slow; firing all 100 at once overloads the browser or the server. A concurrency limiter keeps at most limit running at the same time.
Each task is a function that returns a promise (not a promise), so nothing starts until the limiter decides. As soon as one finishes, the next one starts.
The final result is an array in the original task order, and the whole thing rejects if any task fails.

steps: Keep next (index of the next task to start) and a results array.
Write worker(): while there are tasks left, take index i = next++, await tasks[i](), store results[i].
Start min(limit, tasks.length) workers at once. Each worker keeps pulling tasks until none are left, so at most limit run together.
Return Promise.all(workers).then(() => results); a failing task rejects the whole promise.
how.diagram:
limit 2, tasks A(30ms) B(10ms) C(10ms) D(10ms)
t=0   worker1: A        worker2: B
t=10  worker2: B done -> starts C
t=20  worker2: C done -> starts D
t=30  worker1: A done -> nothing left
t=30  worker2: D done -> all done -> [A, B, C, D] in task order

where: Stay under a rate limit by capping parallel requests.
Tools run N jobs in parallel (like make -j4).
A handful of independent calls: plain Promise.all is simpler.

think.q: Why are tasks given as functions (() => fetch(url)) and not as promises (fetch(url))?
opts: A promise has already started its work; only a function lets the limiter decide when to start
why: Calling fetch(url) starts the request immediately. A list of 100 promises means 100 requests are already running.
Wrapping each in a function delays the start until the limiter calls it.

think.q: limit 2, tasks taking 30, 10, 10, 10 ms. About how long does the whole run take?
why: Task 1 runs 0–30 ms. Tasks 2, 3, 4 run back-to-back on the other slot: 0–10, 10–20, 20–30.
Both slots finish at about 30 ms.

think.q:
async function run(tasks, limit) {
  const out = []
  for (let i = 0; i < tasks.length; i += limit) {
    const batch = tasks.slice(i, i + limit).map(t => t())
    out.push(...(await Promise.all(batch)))
  }
  return out
}
It is correct, but what is wasteful?
opts: It waits for the whole batch: one slow task blocks the free slots until the batch ends
why: Batches leave slots idle. With a 30 ms task and three 1 ms tasks, the next batch still waits 30 ms.
A worker pool starts the next task as soon as any slot frees up.

think.q: Inside a worker, why is const i = next++ safe even though several workers share next?
opts: JS runs one piece of code at a time; workers only switch at await, so next++ is never interrupted
It is not safe; you need a mutex
why: There is one thread. A worker reads and increments next in one synchronous step before it awaits.
So two workers can never take the same index.

problems.pseudo:
runWithConcurrency(tasks, limit):
  results = new Array(tasks.length)
  next = 0
  worker():
    while next < tasks.length:
      i = next; next++
      results[i] = await tasks[i]()
  workers = start min(limit, tasks.length) workers
  await Promise.all(workers)        // rejects if any task rejects
  return results
watch: How do you make sure at most limit tasks run at the same time?
How does each result land at its original index?
What happens to the outer promise when one task fails?

what: === compares objects by reference: two different objects with the same content are not equal. deepEqual compares by content, all the way down.
It must handle the special cases: NaN equals NaN, Dates by their time, RegExps by source and flags, Maps and Sets by their entries, and arrays vs plain objects are not the same.
It is what test libraries use for toEqual, and what you need to answer "did this state really change?".

steps: If Object.is(a, b) → true (covers same reference, equal primitives and NaN).
If either is not an object (or is null) → false. If their prototypes differ → false (so [] is not {}).
Date: compare getTime(). RegExp: compare source and flags.
Map: same size, and every key in a exists in b with a deep-equal value. Set: same size, and every value in a has a deep-equal partner in b.
Arrays and objects: same own keys (count and names), then recurse on each value.
how.diagram:
deepEqual({ a: [1, { b: 2 }] }, { a: [1, { b: 2 }] })
  objects, same keys [a]
    arrays, same length
      1 vs 1        -> Object.is: true
      {b:2} vs {b:2} -> objects, same keys [b] -> 2 vs 2 true
=> true

where: Skip work when new props are deeply the same (use carefully: deep checks cost time).
Hot paths with big objects: prefer immutable updates and a cheap === check.

think.q: console.log(NaN === NaN, Object.is(NaN, NaN), Object.is(0, -0))
why: Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself, which deepEqual wants.
It also says 0 and -0 differ; this lesson keeps that strict behaviour.

think.q: console.log(JSON.stringify({ a: 1, b: 2 }) === JSON.stringify({ b: 2, a: 1 }))
why: JSON text depends on key order, so equal objects can produce different strings.
JSON also drops undefined, turns Dates into strings and cannot see Map/Set content. It is not a deep equal.

think.q:
function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (typeof a !== "object") return a === b
  return Object.keys(a).every(k => deepEqual(a[k], b[k]))
}
Which pair wrongly returns true?
why: It only checks the keys of a. Extra keys in b are never seen.
Compare the key counts (or check both directions) first.

think.q: Why compare prototypes first?
opts: So that [] and {}, or a Date and a plain object, are not called equal just because they have no own keys
why: An empty array and an empty object both have zero own keys.
Checking Object.getPrototypeOf tells them apart.

problems.pseudo:
deepEqual(a, b):
  if Object.is(a, b) -> true
  if a or b is not an object, or is null -> false
  if prototypes differ -> false
  Date   -> compare getTime()
  RegExp -> compare source and flags
  Map    -> same size; every [k, v] of a: b.has(k) and deepEqual(v, b.get(k))
  Set    -> same size; every value of a has some deep-equal value in b
  keysA = own keys of a, keysB = own keys of b
  if lengths differ -> false
  every key k: b has k and deepEqual(a[k], b[k])
watch: What does NaN === NaN give, and what do you want?
How do you notice extra keys in b?
Which types need their own rule instead of comparing keys?

reqs: Primitives compare with Object.is (so NaN equals NaN).
Arrays and plain objects: same keys and deeply equal values; key order does not matter.
Arrays and objects are never equal to each other; different prototypes are not equal.

Map by entries; Set by values (order does not matter).

notes: Object.is as the first line handles same references, equal primitives and NaN.
Prototype check stops [] vs {} and Date vs object from looking equal.
Key count plus "b has every key of a" catches extra and missing keys.
Special types (Date, RegExp, Map, Set) need their own rule; their data is not in own keys.

what: Networks fail for a moment all the time. retry calls an async function, and if it fails, waits and tries again, up to retries more times.
The wait doubles each time (exponential backoff): 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms… so a struggling server gets breathing room instead of a flood.
Some errors are not worth retrying (a 404, a wrong password). A shouldRetry(err) function lets the caller stop at once for those.

steps: Loop with an attempt counter from 0.
Try await fn(attempt); on success, return the value.
On failure: if attempt === retries or shouldRetry(err) is false, throw the error.
Otherwise wait delay * 2 ** attempt ms, increase attempt, and go again.
how.diagram:
retries = 3, delay = 100
try #0  fail -> wait 100
try #1  fail -> wait 200
try #2  fail -> wait 400
try #3  fail -> no retries left -> throw the last error
total calls = retries + 1 = 4

where: Queue workers retry failed jobs with backoff.
Payment or email providers that sometimes time out.
Non-idempotent actions (charging a card) unless the API supports an idempotency key: a retry could do it twice.

think.q: With retries: 3, how many times can fn be called at most?
why: One first try plus 3 retries = 4 calls.
Off-by-one here is the most common bug in retry code.

think.q: Delay 100 ms, 3 retries, every call fails at once. Roughly how long until retry rejects?
why: There is no wait after the last failure; it throws right away.

think.q:
async function retry(fn, n) {
  try { return fn() } catch (e) {
    if (n === 0) throw e
    return retry(fn, n - 1)
  }
}
Why does it never retry an async failure?
opts: Recursion is not allowed with async
return fn() returns the promise without awaiting it, so the catch never sees the rejection
why: A rejected promise is not a thrown error until you await it inside the try.
Write return await fn().

think.q: Thousands of clients fail at the same moment and all retry after exactly 100, 200, 400 ms. What problem appears, and the common fix?
opts: They all hit the server together again ("thundering herd"); add random jitter to each delay
why: Synchronised retries come back as synchronised spikes.
Jitter (for example a random value between 0 and the delay) spreads them out.

what: chain(data) gives you an object with filter, map, sort and take. Each one only records the step and returns the chain, so you can keep calling. Nothing runs until value().
That is lazy evaluation. Done well, it also means less work: chain(million).map(f).take(3).value() should call f only 3 times, because items flow through the steps one at a time.
Generators are perfect for this: each step is a generator that pulls items from the step before it.

steps: Keep an array ops of recorded steps; every method pushes one and returns the chain.
Write one generator per step: filter yields items that pass, map yields fn(item), take yields the first n and then stops.
sort needs all items before it can yield anything: collect into an array, copy, sort, yield.
value(): start with the data, wrap it step by step (seq = step(seq, arg)), then spread the final generator into an array.
how.diagram:
chain([1..1000000]).map(x => x * 2).filter(x => x % 3 === 0).take(2).value()

pull from take -> pull from filter -> pull from map -> pull from data
  1 -> 2 (no)  2 -> 4 (no)  3 -> 6 (yes, #1)
  4 -> 8 (no)  5 -> 10 (no) 6 -> 12 (yes, #2) -> take stops
map ran only 6 times, not 1,000,000

where: Knex / Prisma record .where().orderBy().limit() and run once.
Process huge or endless data piece by piece.
Tiny arrays used once: plain arr.filter().map() is simpler and fast enough.

let calls = 0
const r = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5].map(x => { calls++; return x * 2 }).slice(0, 2)
console.log(r.join(","), calls)
why: Array methods are eager: map processes all 5 items before slice keeps 2.
A lazy chain with take(2) would call the mapper only twice.

think.q:
function* nums() { let i = 0; while (true) yield i++ }
const it = nums()
console.log(it.next().value, it.next().value)
why: A generator runs only until the next yield, then pauses.
That is why an endless generator is fine: you only pull what you need.

think.q:
sort(cmp) { ops.push(arr => arr.sort(cmp)); return this }
with value() starting from data itself. What is wrong?
opts: Array sort works in place, so value() reorders the caller's original array
sort must be the last step
why: The source data belongs to the caller; a query must not change it.
Copy first: [...arr].sort(cmp).

think.q: Why can sort not be lazy like map?
opts: It can; sort is lazy too
To know the first item in order, you must see every item first
why: The smallest item might be the very last one in the input.
So sort collects everything, then yields in order. Steps before it still run lazily.

problems.pseudo:
chain(data):
  ops = []
  api.filter(fn) = push ['filter', fn]; return api
  api.map(fn)    = push ['map', fn];    return api
  api.sort(cmp)  = push ['sort', cmp];  return api
  api.take(n)    = push ['take', n];    return api
  api.value():
    seq = data
    for [type, arg] of ops: seq = generator[type](seq, arg)
    return [...seq]

generators:
  filter(src, fn): for x of src: if fn(x) yield x
  map(src, fn):    for x of src: yield fn(x)
  take(src, n):    if n <= 0 return; count; for x of src: yield x; if ++count >= n return
  sort(src, cmp):  yield* [...src].sort(cmp)
watch: When exactly do the callbacks run?
How does take(3) stop the steps before it from doing more work?
Does value() change the original data, or give a different result the second time?

reqs: Each method records the step and returns the chain (chainable).
No callback runs before value().
value() applies the steps in order and returns an array.
Items flow one at a time: take(n) stops earlier steps from processing more items.
The source data is never changed, and value() can be called again with the same result.

// expected: [30, 50, 80]

checks.verify: const c = chain([1]); assert(c.filter(() => true) === c, 'filter should return the chain'); assert(chain([]).map((x) => x).value().length === 0, 'empty data'); assert(chain([1, 2]).take(0).value().length === 0, 'take(0) should give []'); assert(chain([1, 2]).value().join() === '1,2', 'no steps should return the items')

notes: Methods only record; value() builds a generator pipeline and drains it.
Generators pull one item at a time, so take naturally stops the work before it.
sort is a barrier: it must see everything. It copies, so the source is safe.
A fresh pipeline per value() call makes results repeatable.

problems.signature: withTimeout(promise, ms, options) / delay(ms) / class TimeoutError

what: A promise can wait forever: a server that never answers, a lost callback. withTimeout(p, ms) gives you a promise that settles like p, or rejects with a TimeoutError if p takes longer than ms.
Optionally it resolves with a fallback value instead of failing (show cached data, a default).
Do it cleanly: clear the timer when p wins, so nothing keeps running, and do not create unhandled rejections from the losing side.

steps: delay(ms): new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms)).
class TimeoutError extends Error with name = "TimeoutError".
withTimeout: return a new Promise. Start a timer that, after ms, resolves with the fallback (if one was given) or rejects with a TimeoutError.
Attach to p: on success or failure, clearTimeout and pass the result or error through. The first one to settle wins.
how.diagram:
withTimeout(fetchUser(), 100)
case 1: fetchUser ok at 40ms   -> clear timer -> resolve(user)
case 2: fetchUser slow (500ms) -> timer at 100ms -> reject(TimeoutError)
                                   later result is ignored
case 3: with { fallback: [] }  -> timer at 100ms -> resolve([])

where: Give up on a slow API after 5 s and show a retry button.
Fail a test that hangs instead of waiting forever.
Recommendations take too long? Show the page without them (fallback).
A timeout does not stop the underlying work. To really cancel a fetch, also use an AbortController.

think.q: The timeout fires first. What happens to the original fetch?
opts: It keeps running in the background; its result is just ignored
why: Promises cannot be cancelled. The race only decides which result you see.
Pass an AbortSignal to fetch and abort it on timeout to really stop the request.

think.q:
Promise.race([new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r("slow"), 50)), "now"]).then(console.log)
What is printed?
why: A plain value in race counts as already resolved, so it wins.
That is also why an already-settled promise beats a timer of 0 ms.

think.q:
function withTimeout(p, ms) {
  const timer = new Promise((_, rej) => setTimeout(() => rej(new Error("timeout")), ms))
  return Promise.race([p, timer])
}
p resolves in 10 ms, ms is 60000. What is wrong?
opts: The 60-second timer keeps running after p wins: it holds the process open and fires a rejection nobody handles
why: The timer is never cleared. In Node it keeps the process alive; when it fires, the rejected promise has no handler.
Clear the timer when p settles.

think.q: Why make a TimeoutError class instead of new Error("timeout")?
opts: Callers can tell a timeout apart from other errors with instanceof (for example, retry only on timeouts)
why: Checking messages is fragile. err instanceof TimeoutError is clear and safe.
Setting name also makes logs readable.

problems.pseudo:
delay(ms) = new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, ms))
class TimeoutError extends Error: name = 'TimeoutError'

withTimeout(p, ms, { fallback } = {}):
  hasFallback = 'fallback' was passed
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    timer = setTimeout(() =>
      hasFallback ? resolve(fallback) : reject(new TimeoutError('Timed out after ' + ms + 'ms')), ms)
    Promise.resolve(p).then(
      v => { clearTimeout(timer); resolve(v) },
      e => { clearTimeout(timer); reject(e) }))
watch: What happens to the timer when the promise wins?
How will a caller recognise a timeout error?
How do you tell "no fallback" from "fallback is undefined"?

reqs: If the promise settles first, its value or error passes through unchanged.
If it takes longer than ms, reject with a TimeoutError (a subclass of Error, name "TimeoutError").
With a fallback option, resolve with it on timeout instead.
Clear the timer when the promise wins (no timer left running).
delay(ms) resolves after about ms milliseconds.

checks.test: const t = Date.now(); await delay(30); console.log(Date.now() - t >= 25) // expected: true
checks.verify: const t = Date.now(); const r = delay(30); assert(r instanceof Promise, 'delay must return a promise'); await r; assert(Date.now() - t >= 25, 'did not wait')
checks.gap: return new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms)).

checks.test: withTimeout(delay(10).then(() => 'data'), 100).then(console.log) // expected: data
checks.verify: const v = await withTimeout(new Promise((r) => setTimeout(() => r('data'), 10)), 100); assert(v === 'data', 'got ' + v)
checks.gap: Resolve with the promise's value when it settles first.

checks.t: Rejects with TimeoutError when slow

checks.verify: let e; const t = Date.now(); try { await withTimeout(new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200)), 20) } catch (x) { e = x } assert(e instanceof TimeoutError && e instanceof Error, 'should be a TimeoutError'); assert(e.name === 'TimeoutError', 'name is ' + (e && e.name)); assert(Date.now() - t < 150, 'should not wait for the slow promise')

checks.t: Errors from the promise pass through unchanged
checks.test: withTimeout(Promise.reject(new Error('404')), 100).catch((e) => console.log(e.message)) // expected: 404
checks.verify: const err = new Error('404'); let e; try { await withTimeout(Promise.reject(err), 100) } catch (x) { e = x } assert(e === err, 'should be the same error')

checks.t: fallback resolves instead of failing
checks.test: withTimeout(delay(200), 20, { fallback: [] }).then((v) => console.log(v)) // expected: []
checks.verify: const v = await withTimeout(new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200)), 20, { fallback: 'cached' }); assert(v === 'cached', 'got ' + v); const u = await withTimeout(new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 200)), 10, { fallback: undefined }); assert(u === undefined, 'an explicit undefined fallback should resolve')

await withTimeout(Promise.resolve(1), 60000)
checks.verify: const orig = globalThis.clearTimeout; let cleared = 0; globalThis.clearTimeout = (id) => { cleared++; return orig(id) }; try { const v = await withTimeout(Promise.resolve(1), 60000); assert(v === 1, 'should resolve with 1'); assert(cleared >= 1, 'the timer was not cleared') } finally { globalThis.clearTimeout = orig }
checks.gap: Call clearTimeout(timer) in both handlers of the original promise.

notes: A new Promise with a timer and the original's handlers is a race you control: you can clean up.
clearTimeout when the original wins, so no stray timer fires or keeps Node alive.
A custom error class makes timeouts easy to detect with instanceof.
A timeout does not cancel the work itself; pair it with AbortController for fetch.

problems.signature: class CircuitBreaker(fn, options) { call, state, reset } / class CircuitOpenError

what: When a service is down, retrying again and again just makes it worse and makes your users wait for timeouts. A circuit breaker wraps the call and, after several failures in a row, stops calling for a while and fails fast instead.

Three states: CLOSED (normal, calls go through), OPEN (calls fail at once with a CircuitOpenError, for a cooldown), and HALF_OPEN (after the cooldown, let one trial call through: success closes the circuit, failure opens it again).
The name comes from the electrical breaker in your house: it cuts the power to protect the system, and you can try to switch it back on later.

steps: Store state = "CLOSED", a failure counter, and openedAt.
call(...args): if OPEN and the cooldown has passed, switch to HALF_OPEN. If still OPEN (or HALF_OPEN with a trial already running), reject with CircuitOpenError without calling fn.
Otherwise call fn. On success: reset failures to 0 and set CLOSED.
On failure: in HALF_OPEN, open again at once; in CLOSED, count it and open when the count reaches failureThreshold. Always re-throw the original error.
reset() forces CLOSED with zero failures.
how.diagram:
CLOSED --(threshold failures in a row)--> OPEN
  ^                                         |
  |                                 cooldown passes
  |                                         v
  +----(trial call succeeds)---------- HALF_OPEN
                 trial call fails -> OPEN again (new cooldown)

where: Stop calling a failing payment service; show "try again later" at once.
Stop hammering an API that returns 503; retry after a pause.
Errors caused by the request itself (400, validation) should not count as service failures.

think.q: Threshold 3. Results: fail, fail, success, fail, fail. What is the state?
why: The success in the middle resets the counter, so there are only 2 failures in a row at the end.
Breakers count consecutive failures (or a rate over a window), not a lifetime total.

think.q: While OPEN, why not call the function and just ignore its result?
opts: It would be the same thing
The point is to send no traffic: the failing service gets time to recover and callers get an instant answer
why: Every call to a dead service costs a timeout and adds load.
Failing fast protects both sides.

think.q: In HALF_OPEN, 50 requests arrive at the same moment. What should happen?
opts: Only a few trial calls (often 1) go through; the rest fail fast until the trial decides
why: Letting everyone through would flood a service that might still be broken.
One (or a few) probes test it safely.

think.q: On failure in HALF_OPEN the code does this.failures++ and opens only when failures >= threshold. What goes wrong?
opts: A failed trial does not reopen the circuit, so traffic flows to a service that is still down
why: The trial is the test. If it fails, the service is not healthy: go straight back to OPEN with a fresh cooldown.
Counting it like a normal failure would need several more failed calls to a dead service before opening again.

problems.pseudo:
class CircuitOpenError extends Error

class CircuitBreaker(fn, { failureThreshold = 3, cooldown = 1000 }):
  state = 'CLOSED'; failures = 0; openedAt = 0; trial = false

  async call(...args):
    if state == 'OPEN' and now - openedAt >= cooldown: state = 'HALF_OPEN'
    if state == 'OPEN' or (state == 'HALF_OPEN' and trial running):
      throw new CircuitOpenError
    if state == 'HALF_OPEN': trial = true
    try:
      result = await fn(...args)
      failures = 0; state = 'CLOSED'; return result
    catch err:
      if state == 'HALF_OPEN' or ++failures >= failureThreshold:
        state = 'OPEN'; openedAt = now
      throw err
    finally: trial = false

  reset(): state = 'CLOSED'; failures = 0
watch: Which event moves OPEN to HALF_OPEN: a timer, or the next call?
What resets the failure count?
What happens when the trial call fails?

build.problem: Build class CircuitBreaker(fn, { failureThreshold, cooldown }) with call(...args), a state property and reset(), plus class CircuitOpenError.
reqs: CLOSED: calls go to fn; its result or error passes through.
After failureThreshold failures in a row → OPEN. A success resets the count.
OPEN: reject at once with CircuitOpenError without calling fn.
After cooldown ms the next call is a trial (HALF_OPEN): success → CLOSED, failure → OPEN again. Only one trial at a time.
reset() → CLOSED with zero failures.

checks.t: CLOSED passes results and errors through
checks.test:
const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async (x) => x * 2)
console.log(await cb.call(21), cb.state) // expected: 42 CLOSED
checks.verify: const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async (x) => x * 2); assert(await cb.call(21) === 42, 'result should pass through'); assert(cb.state === 'CLOSED', 'state ' + cb.state); const bad = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { throw new Error('down') }); let m; try { await bad.call() } catch (e) { m = e.message } assert(m === 'down', 'the original error should pass through')

checks.t: Opens after N failures in a row; a success resets the count
checks.test: // threshold 3: fail, fail, ok, fail, fail -> CLOSED; one more fail -> OPEN
checks.verify: let ok = false; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { if (!ok) throw new Error('x'); return 'y' }, { failureThreshold: 3, cooldown: 1000 }); const tryCall = async () => { try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} }; await tryCall(); await tryCall(); ok = true; await cb.call(); ok = false; await tryCall(); await tryCall(); assert(cb.state === 'CLOSED', 'should still be CLOSED, is ' + cb.state); await tryCall(); assert(cb.state === 'OPEN', 'should be OPEN, is ' + cb.state)
checks.gap: Set failures = 0 on success; open when ++failures >= failureThreshold.

checks.t: OPEN fails fast without calling fn
checks.test: // after opening: call() rejects with CircuitOpenError and fn is not called
checks.verify: let calls = 0; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { calls++; throw new Error('x') }, { failureThreshold: 2, cooldown: 1000 }); for (let i = 0; i < 2; i++) { try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} } const before = calls; let e; try { await cb.call() } catch (x) { e = x } assert(e instanceof CircuitOpenError && e instanceof Error, 'should reject with CircuitOpenError'); assert(calls === before, 'fn must not be called while OPEN')
checks.gap: Check the state first and throw new CircuitOpenError(...) before calling fn.

checks.t: After the cooldown a successful trial closes it
checks.test: // cooldown 40ms: wait, then call() -> trial succeeds -> CLOSED
checks.verify: let ok = false; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { if (!ok) throw new Error('x'); return 'back' }, { failureThreshold: 1, cooldown: 40 }); try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} assert(cb.state === 'OPEN', 'should be OPEN'); await sleep(60); ok = true; assert(await cb.call() === 'back', 'trial should run'); assert(cb.state === 'CLOSED', 'should close after a good trial, is ' + cb.state)
checks.gap: When OPEN and Date.now() - openedAt >= cooldown, switch to HALF_OPEN and let the call through.

checks.t: A failed trial opens it again with a new cooldown
checks.test: // trial fails -> OPEN, and calls right after still fail fast
checks.verify: let calls = 0; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { calls++; throw new Error('x') }, { failureThreshold: 1, cooldown: 40 }); try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} await sleep(60); try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} assert(calls === 2, 'the trial should call fn'); assert(cb.state === 'OPEN', 'should be OPEN again, is ' + cb.state); let e; try { await cb.call() } catch (x) { e = x } assert(e instanceof CircuitOpenError, 'should fail fast again'); assert(calls === 2, 'fn called during the new cooldown')
checks.gap: On failure in HALF_OPEN, set OPEN and a fresh openedAt straight away.

checks.t: Only one trial call at a time
checks.test: // HALF_OPEN: two calls at once -> one runs, the other gets CircuitOpenError
checks.verify: let calls = 0; let fail = true; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { calls++; if (fail) throw new Error('x'); await sleep(30); return 'ok' }, { failureThreshold: 1, cooldown: 30 }); try { await cb.call() } catch (e) {} fail = false; await sleep(50); const [a, b] = await Promise.allSettled([cb.call(), cb.call()]); assert(a.status === 'fulfilled' && a.value === 'ok', 'the first call should be the trial'); assert(b.status === 'rejected' && b.reason instanceof CircuitOpenError, 'the second should fail fast'); assert(calls === 2, 'fn called ' + calls + ' times')
checks.gap: Keep a trial flag: set it when the trial starts and clear it in finally.

checks.t: reset() closes the circuit
checks.test: cb.reset(); console.log(cb.state) // expected: CLOSED
checks.verify: let calls = 0; const cb = new CircuitBreaker(async () => { calls++; return calls }, { failureThreshold: 1, cooldown: 10000 }); cb.state = 'OPEN'; cb.openedAt = Date.now(); cb.reset(); assert(cb.state === 'CLOSED', 'state ' + cb.state); assert(await cb.call() === 1, 'calls should go through after reset')
checks.gap: reset() sets state = "CLOSED" and failures = 0.

notes: The move from OPEN to HALF_OPEN happens lazily, on the next call after the cooldown: no timers needed.
Count consecutive failures; any success resets the counter.
A failed trial reopens immediately with a fresh cooldown.
A trial flag cleared in finally keeps HALF_OPEN to one probe at a time.
Always re-throw the real error, so callers still see why the call failed.

Use a failure rate over the last N calls instead of a consecutive count.
Add an isFailure(err) option so 4xx errors do not trip the breaker.

problems.signature: class Stopwatch({ now }) { start, pause, reset, lap, getElapsed, getLaps, onTick }

what: A stopwatch measures time while it runs. You can pause and start again, record laps, and reset.

Do not count ticks of a timer: setInterval is never exact. Store the moment you started and the time already banked before the last pause, and compute elapsed = banked + (now − startedAt) whenever someone asks.
A clock function (now) is passed in, so tests can control time. UI updates come from onTick(cb), which only reads the elapsed time.

steps: State: running, startedAt, banked (ms from earlier runs), laps, lastLapAt.
start(): if already running, do nothing; else startedAt = now(), running = true.
pause(): if running, banked += now() − startedAt, running = false.
getElapsed(): banked + (running ? now() − startedAt : 0). lap(): total = getElapsed(), split = total − lastLapAt, store and update lastLapAt.
onTick(cb, every): a setInterval that calls cb(getElapsed()) only while running; return a function that clears it.
how.diagram:
t=0     start        banked 0
t=3000  pause        banked 3000
t=8000  start        startedAt 8000   (the 5s paused are not counted)
t=10000 getElapsed   3000 + (10000 - 8000) = 5000
t=10000 lap          { lap: 1, split: 5000, total: 5000 }

where: Lap times for runs and workouts.
Level timers that pause with the game.
Measure how long steps of a task take.
Counting down to a deadline: that is a countdown timer (same idea, reversed).

think.q: Why compute elapsed from now() − startedAt instead of adding 100 every 100 ms tick?
opts: Timers can fire late (busy thread, background tab), so counting ticks drifts; real timestamps do not
setInterval does not exist in Node
why: A tab in the background may run your interval once per second or less.
Timestamps are always right no matter how late the tick is.

think.q: Start at 0, pause at 4000, start at 6000, pause at 7000. What is the elapsed time?
why: First run 4000 ms is banked; second run adds 7000 − 6000 = 1000.
The 2000 ms paused gap is not counted.

think.q: What is a lap "split"?
opts: Time since the previous lap (or since start, for the first lap)
why: Split = this lap's length. Total = time since the very start.
Keep lastLapAt (in elapsed time, not clock time) to compute it.

think.q:
start() {
  this.startedAt = this.now()
  this.running = true
}
Someone calls start() twice. What breaks?
opts: The second call moves startedAt forward, so time between the two calls is lost
why: Elapsed is measured from startedAt; resetting it while running throws away time.
Guard with if (this.running) return.

problems.pseudo:
class Stopwatch({ now = Date.now }):
  running = false; startedAt = 0; banked = 0; laps = []; lastLapAt = 0

  start(): if running return; startedAt = now(); running = true
  pause(): if not running return; banked += now() - startedAt; running = false
  reset(): running = false; banked = 0; laps = []; lastLapAt = 0
  getElapsed(): banked + (running ? now() - startedAt : 0)
  lap():
    total = getElapsed(); split = total - lastLapAt; lastLapAt = total
    laps.push({ lap: laps.length + 1, split, total }); return that lap
  getLaps(): copy of laps
  onTick(cb, every = 100):
    id = setInterval(() => if running: cb(getElapsed()), every)
    return () => clearInterval(id)
watch: Where does the time from before a pause live?
What should a second start() do?
Is a lap split measured in clock time or elapsed time?

lap() returns and stores { lap, split, total }.
reset() stops, zeroes the time and clears laps.

problems.signature: class ConsistentHashing({ vnodes }) { addServer, removeServer, getServer, size } / hash(str)

what: You spread keys (users, cache entries) over N servers. The simple way, hash(key) % N, breaks badly when N changes: going from 4 to 5 servers moves almost every key.

Consistent hashing puts servers on a ring of numbers (0 to 2³²−1). A key goes to the first server marker clockwise from its hash. Adding a server only takes the keys just before its markers: about 1/N of all keys move.
Each server gets many virtual nodes (say 150 markers) so the load spreads evenly instead of in a few big arcs.

steps: hash(str): a fast 32-bit hash (FNV-1a) with a final mix step, returning an unsigned integer.
addServer(name): for i = 0 … vnodes−1, add a marker { pos: hash(name + "#" + i), server: name }; keep the ring sorted by pos.
removeServer(name): drop every marker of that server.
getServer(key): h = hash(key); binary-search the first marker with pos >= h; if none, wrap to marker 0. Return its server (or null if the ring is empty).
how.diagram:
ring 0 ............................................. 2^32
markers:   A#3   B#0     A#1    C#2    B#7    C#0   A#5
key k:            ^ hash(k)
                  -> first marker clockwise is A#1 -> server A
add D: its markers cut a few arcs; only keys in those arcs move to D

where: Memcached/Redis clients pick a node per key; adding a node keeps most hits.
Cassandra and DynamoDB place data on a ring.
Sticky routing of a user to the same backend.
A fixed number of servers that never changes: plain modulo is fine.

think.q: With hash(key) % N, roughly what share of keys move when N goes from 4 to 5?
why: A key stays only if h % 4 === h % 5, which is true for about 1 in 5 keys. So around 80% move.
With consistent hashing only about 1/5 (20%) move: the ones the new server takes.

think.q: Why give each server ~150 virtual nodes instead of 1 marker?
opts: One marker per server makes uneven arcs, so some servers get far more keys; many markers average it out
why: Random positions leave big and small gaps. With many markers per server, each server owns many small arcs and the totals even out.
More vnodes = better balance, at the cost of a bigger ring.

think.q: A key's hash is larger than every marker on the ring. Which server gets it?
opts: The server of the last marker
The server of the first (smallest) marker: the ring wraps around
why: It is a circle: after the top value you continue from 0.
In code: if the binary search finds no marker, use index 0.

think.q:
let moved = 0
for (let h = 0; h < 1000; h++) if (h % 4 !== h % 5) moved++
console.log(moved)
why: Only values where both remainders match stay: 0–3 of every 20, so 200 of 1000 stay and 800 move.
That is the problem consistent hashing solves.

problems.pseudo:
hash(str): FNV-1a 32-bit over the characters, then a mix step; return unsigned

class ConsistentHashing({ vnodes = 150 }):
  ring = []                // sorted [{ pos, server }]
  servers = new Set()
  addServer(name):
    if servers has name -> return
    for i in 0..vnodes-1: ring.push({ pos: hash(name + '#' + i), server: name })
    sort ring by pos; servers.add(name)
  removeServer(name): ring = ring without name's markers; servers.delete(name)
  getServer(key):
    if ring empty -> null
    h = hash(key)
    binary search smallest index with ring[i].pos >= h
    if none -> i = 0
    return ring[i].server
  size = ring.length
watch: What happens to keys hashed after the last marker?
How do you find the next marker fast (not a loop over the whole ring)?
What should adding the same server twice do?

build.problem: Build class ConsistentHashing({ vnodes }) with addServer, removeServer, getServer(key) and a size getter, plus a hash(str) function.
reqs: hash(str) returns the same unsigned 32-bit integer for the same string.
Each server places vnodes markers (default 150); size is the number of markers. Adding a server twice changes nothing.
getServer(key) returns the server of the first marker clockwise from hash(key) (wrapping), or null with no servers. Use binary search.
Adding a server moves only about 1/N of the keys, all of them to the new server.
Removing a server moves only the keys it owned.

notes: Servers and keys share one hash space; a key belongs to the next server marker clockwise.
Virtual nodes turn a few big uneven arcs into many small ones: balanced load.
Binary search over the sorted markers makes lookups O(log M).
Adding or removing a server only touches the arcs next to its own markers.
